list.listitem: Wireless video capsule endoscopy (VCE) is a significant advancement in GI imaging. The capsule (see ) is a self-contained camera and antenna that transmits images to a sensor array/data recorder; the recorded images are captured by the data recorder and downloaded to a computer workstation where they can be viewed by a physician. is a summary of VCE indications and current procedural terminology codes.
The VCE capsule captures 2 images per second during 8 hours of its battery life for small bowel studies and 18 images per second during 30 minutes of its battery life for esophageal studies.

In patients at risk for capsule retention (e.g., Crohn's disease, suspected small bowel stenosis), a patency capsule can help confirm small bowel passage before performing VCE. The Agile patency capsule is composed of lactose with barium and includes a radiofrequency identification tag. This capsule remains intact for a minimum of 30 hours and then disintegrates.
The AdvanCE capsule delivery system deliveries the VCE capsule into the small bowel of patients with known dysphagia, gastroparesis, or abnormal upper GI anatomy.

The first commercially available VCE was in 2001. Currently, the following capsules have the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval: CapsoCam SV-1®,Endocapsule 10®, PillCam Colon2®, MiroCam 4000®, PillCam SB3®, while OMOM Capsule2® has yet to be approved. They differ in the number and size of cameras, the frame of the field, and the number of frames per second taken.

Obscure GI bleeding accounts for 66% of the indications for VCE. Other indications include chronic abdominal pain or diarrhea 10.6%, Crohn's disease (CD) 10.4%, small bowel tumor 3.5%, and celiac disease 1.7%.

There are certain limitations to VCE that should be taken into consideration when approaching the patient: taking biopsies is not possible; administering therapeutic drugs in not possible; and locating the exact position of a GI lesion is difficult.
The USPSTF has not approved VCE as a modality for colorectal cancer screening.

Other modalities for viewing the small intestine have similar or inferior diagnostic yield compared to small capsule endoscopy (60%): double balloon endoscopy 57%, small bowel radiography 37%, and push enteroscopy 35%.

A magnetically controlled capsule endoscopy (MCCE) has been introduced for the visualization of the stomach and esophagus. MCCE is a good alternative to endoscopy for patients who refuse the more invasive procedure.

VCE cost-effectiveness has been studied in colorectal cancer but not IBD. It has been proposed by the British National Health Service that it could be cost-effective in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients in the long-term when compared to the conventional magnetic resonance enterography (MRE) with or without colonoscopy, as it can result in a delay of the surgical interventions in those patients who are early monitored with VCE and started biologic therapy.

Movable capsule can be limited by peristalsis of the bowel if only passive movements were allowed, which makes the movement and position of the capsule unpredictable. In addition, rapid motion could lead to poor visualization of parts of the gut. New devices allow for components containing tools for diagnostic sampling or drug release. The size of the capsule even with the tools should not exceed 3.4 cm in length and 1.3 cm in width or diameter.

In children, VCE is used primarily to evaluate suspected small bowel disease after initial testing is nondiagnostic. Common indications include suspected small bowel bleeding or unexplained iron deficiency anemia, suspected or known small bowel Crohn's Disease, and surveillance or evaluation of polyposis syndromes. Reported diagnostic yield for obscure GI bleeding varies widely, from 19% to 95% in small series. VCE may complement MRE in selected children with CD since it directly visualizes small bowel mucosa but does not evaluate transmural or extraluminal pathology. Less common pediatric uses of VCE include detection of small bowel tumors and evaluation of celiac disease.
VCE is an option in patients with a presumptive diagnosis of small bowel bleeding after upper endoscopy and colonoscopy have failed to identify bleeding source.

The lower rate of detection of obscure bleeding by VCE, as compared to conventional GI endoscopy, could be attributed to the absence of various intervention maneuvers to remove air and secretions (bile, food, and mucus) from the bowel, which may hinder the visualization by the camera.
A pooled analysis showed a sensitivity of 63% to 87% for small bowel VCE, 28% for enteroscopy, and 8% to 13% for radiography.
In a pooled analysis of 10 studies, the diagnostic yield of VCE was similar to that of double-balloon enteroscopy in patients with obscure GI bleeding.

Common small bowel VCE findings for obscure GI bleeding include angiodysplasia, Crohn’s disease, Celiac disease, small bowel tumors, small bowel diverticula, infections, and small bowel Dieulafoy’s lesions.

VCE and simple balloon enteroscopy (SBE) are complementary tests for evaluating suspected small bowel disease. VCE is noninvasive and is often used first in stable patients with suspected small bowel bleeding, especially when a vascular lesion is suspected. SBE is invasive but allows biopsy and therapeutic intervention, and may be preferred when tissue diagnosis or treatment is needed. In one meta-analysis, SBE had a higher detection rate than VCE for Crohn's disease and a modestly higher overall detection rate for small bowel bleeding, whereas VCE performed better in detecting vascular lesions.

Pan-intestinal VCE, which evaluates both the small bowel and colon, has been studied as a possible triage test in selected patients with suspected mid- or lower-GI bleeding, especially after a nondiagnostic upper endoscopy. In small studies, pan-intestinal VCE identified bleeding sources and helped determine which patients required therapeutic endoscopy, potentially reducing unnecessary invasive procedures. However, evidence remains limited, and pan-intestinal VCE is not yet a routine first-line test for most patients with GI bleeding.
Small bowel tumors account for 1% to 3% of all GI neoplasms.
In a multicenter study involving 5129 patients with 124 small bowel tumors, small bowel VCE found GI stromal tumors (32%), adenocarcinomas (20%), carcinoids (15%), and metastatic tumors (10%).

section.heading: Evaluation of the site and extent of Crohn's disease

list.listitem: VCE is the most accurate test for detecting the presence and extent of small bowel Crohn’s disease.
The diagnostic yield of VCE was 63% compared with 23% for small bowel radiography in 9 studies involving 250 patients.
The diagnostic yield of VCE was 61% compared with 46% for colonoscopy with ileoscopy in 4 studies involving 114 patients.
The diagnostic yield of VCE was 69% compared with 30% for CT in 3 studies involving 93 patients.

The European Crohn’s and Colitis Organisation (ECCO) guidelines for the diagnosis and follow up of that the diagnosis and monitoring of CD and colitis depend mainly on conventional endoscopy. Although VCE showed promising results in monitoring treatment, the data is still sparse. One study enrolled 187 patients and demonstrated that 52% of the patients with CD had a change in management due to the VCE findings.

VCE is also used in ulcerative colitis. A colon cam was introduced in 2006, colon cleansing is a premandatory step for the use of this cam. Since then the frequency of pictures has been increased from 4 to 35 images/second. A specific Capsule Scoring of Ulcerative Colitis (CSUC) was introduced in 2018, it is not yet validated despite being the only capsule score for UC.
In 2017 the American Gastroenterology Association (AGA) recommmeded VCE for CD patients if they are suspected to have active disease despite normal ileocolonoscopy and imaging.

Bowel preparation can improve mucosal visualization during VCE, but the optimal preparation regimen for patients with CD is uncertain. Common approaches include a low-residue or clear-liquid diet before the procedure, fasting before capsule ingestion, and/or polyethylene glycol-based preparation. Because protocols vary and evidence is limited, patients should follow the preparation instructions provided by the center performing the study.

In a small randomized trial of patients with small bowel CD in corticosteroid-free clinical remission, VCE-guided treatment optimization every 6 months reduced clinical flares over 24 months compared with standard care. These findings suggest that symptoms alone may not reliably reflect inflammatory activity in small bowel CD. However, routine serial VCE monitoring is not yet standard practice and should be determined by the consulting gastroenterologist.

section.type: Evaluation, extent and complications of Celiac disease
section.heading: Evaluation, extent and complications of Celiac disease

list.listitem: VCE demonstrates good sensitivity and specificity for the detection of celiac disease.
Consider VCE in patients with unexplained abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss who have positive tissue transglutaminase and antiendomysium antibodies and negative upper endoscopy with biopsy.

A 2025 meta-analysis found that VCE detected small bowel abnormalities in about 60% of patients with known celiac disease. VCE may be useful in selected patients to evaluate disease extent or complications, but serology and duodenal biopsy remain the standard diagnostic tests.
Esophageal capsule endoscopy (ECE) (see ) is an option for noninvasive evaluation of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) to rule out Barrett’s esophagus (BE).
Four studies have addressed the diagnostic accuracy of ECE for BE compared with standard upper endoscopy. The sensitivity was 77% and specificity ranged from 75% to 100%.

The complication rate was 0.5% involving capsule retention requiring endoscopic removal. No studies have clearly assessed cost-effectiveness or patient satisfaction in the evaluation of chronic GERD for BE.
Esophageal capsule endoscopy (ECE) may be an option for the diagnosis of esophageal varices.

In a meta-analysis, a summary estimate of the sensitivity for detection of esophageal varices was not possible due to the heterogeneity of the studies on ECE, but specificity was 88%. A Cochrane review recommended against the use of ECE for the detection of esophageal varices in patients with cirrhosis, given the methodological shortcomings of the evaluated studies.
VCE is not approved for detection of colon polyps in the United States.

Two small studies (n = 132) compared PillCam Colon with colonoscopy. The sensitivity and specificity of PillCam Colon was inferior to that of colonoscopy for detection of polyps (sensitivity 56%-77% and specificity 69%-70%). In addition, a comprehensive bowel preparation was required.

Two systematic reviews of diagnostic accuracy studies found that colon capsule endoscopy had similar sensitivity and specificity for polyps as colonoscopy when the capsule transited the entire colon, but complete transit rates varied from 57% to 100%.

A RCT comparing colon capsule endoscopy with CT colonography (with colonoscopy as the reference standard) in patients with positive FIT screening tests found a similar senstivity for advanced neoplasia but a higher detection rate for CCE for any lesion.

In hereditary polyposis syndromes, VCE is used mainly for small bowel surveillance in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, beginning at about 8 years of age and repeated every 3 years when VCE is the chosen modality. VCE may identify clinically significant small bowel polyps that require prophylactic removal, but it does not allow biopsy or polypectomy and may miss or mislocalize lesions. Evidence is insufficient to recommend routine VCE surveillance for most other hereditary polyposis syndromes.
The patient should fast for at least 8 hours or administer preprocedure gut-cleansing agents, prokinetic agents, or simethicone.
A phase III RCT conducted on 167 patients showed that high dose simethcone did not provide any significant benefit in improving the capsule visualization, when compared to the standard dose.

In a recent RCT, diving method (by administering extra 500 ml water when the capsule reaches the small intestine and 500 ml per hour till the battery dies) was assessed on 64 patients compared to 76 patients in the control group. The endoscopic scores of images taken in the small bowel significantly improved in the proximal (3.47 vs 3.11) and middle third (3.24 vs 2.78) as compared to the control group. In addition, the completion rate of VCE was significantly improved in the diving versus the control group (92.19% vs 76.32%). However, there was no difference between the two methods in the transit time of the stomach and intestine, along with a similar lesion detection rate.
Fit the patient with sensor array, leads, and recorder.
Activate the VCE capsule by removing it from the package and confirm sensor array/recorder placement by running the capsule over the attached leads.
After obtaining informed consent, have the patient ingest the capsule with 30 to 60 cc of water.
The patient may leave the endoscopy unit or clinic and should take nothing by mouth for 2 hours after capsule ingestion, and then advance their diet to clear liquids for an additional 2 hours.
The patient should return to the endoscopy unit or clinic after 8 hours.
The sensor array, leads, and recorder are removed from the patient and the images are downloaded onto the computer workstation receiver.
The physician then reads the images on a computer workstation with proprietary RAPID software and generates a report of their findings.
It takes an average of 20 to 45 minutes to read and interpret VCE studies.
The capsule usually passes with bowel movement within 24 hours.
Known or suspected GI obstruction, strictures, or fistulas (Agile patency capsule prior to VCE).
Prior abdominal surgeries (consider giving Agile patency capsule prior to VCE).
Dysphagia/swallowing disorders (consider AdvanCE capsule delivery by endoscopy).
Gastroparesis (consider AdvanCE capsule delivery by endoscopy).
Cardiac pacemaker or other implanted electromedical devices (theoretical risk, need to consider on an individual patient basis).
Less than 10 years of age or pregnancy.
Capsule retention occurs in 1.6% of patients with suspected Crohn’s disease and in 13% of patients with known Crohn’s disease.
Capsule retention is only a concern if the capsule fails to reach the cecum when the study is read.
Patients with concern for retained capsule should have plain abdominal radiography performed.
Retained capsules are removed with a balloon enteroscope or surgically.
It should be stressed to the patient prior to the study that if the capsule is retained likely whatever caused its retention (eg, stricture or tumor) should likely be removed surgically anyway.
Have the patient return within 2 to 4 weeks to review results and discuss therapeutic plan.
